# Interviewer Guide — Problem 03: renamed course grades

**This file is interviewer-facing only. Do not share with candidates.**

## Source

Based on a real Berkeleytime bug and fix: commit `9db8b2ffa` ("associated
renamed courses correctly in grades", PR #1130). Berkeleytime looks up grade
distributions by subject + course number. When the campus renames or
renumbers a course (subject and/or number changes, same course
continuously taught), the naive subject+number lookup only finds grade rows
recorded under the *current* identity — every grade row filed under the
course's prior identity is silently missed, so a renamed course appears to
have thin or missing grade history when it actually has a full one, just
under an old label.

The real fix leaned on infrastructure that already existed but wasn't being
used: Berkeleytime's `Section` records are already tagged with a stable
internal `courseId` (sourced from the campus SIS's own stable course
identifier) independent of subject+number. The bug was that several grade
lookup functions (`getGradeDistributionByCourse` and friends, in
`apps/backend/src/modules/grade-distribution/controller.ts`) took
`courseNumber` as a parameter and filtered sections by
`{ subject, courseNumber }` instead of `{ subject, courseId }`. Switching
those call sites to filter by `courseId` fixed it, because `courseId` (unlike
`courseNumber`) doesn't change on rename.

This is worth knowing going in: the "big" design (stable internal ID,
option 3 below) was *already partially built* in Berkeleytime — the data
model had the stable id, but a chunk of query logic wasn't using it. That's
a useful thing to bring up with a candidate who assumes greenfield: in
practice, this class of bug is often "the stable identity exists somewhere
in the system and someone forgot to route a query through it," not "nobody
ever thought about this."

Note also `packages/common/src/models/course.ts` has a `formerDisplayName`
field with a comment `// NOTE: Replace with cs-course-id of former course` —
evidence Berkeleytime's own data model has, at various points, groped toward
a proper alias/history table (design #1 below) and settled for a much
weaker single-string field instead. Good color if a candidate asks "well
what does the real system actually do."

---

## Round 1: System Design discussion guide

### The four designs

Present these as the menu if the candidate gets stuck, but ideally let them
arrive at 2-3 of these unprompted and only introduce the others as
"here's another option — how does it compare?"

**1. Alias / history table.** A separate table storing every subject+number
an entity has ever held, keyed to a stable internal entity id. Historical
records join through the alias table (entity id -> all past identities ->
match historical records recorded under any of them) rather than joining
directly on the current label.
- Pro: handles arbitrary rename counts naturally; auditable (you can see the
  full rename history); relatively contained scope — you're adding a table
  and changing how joins happen, not changing what a "record" fundamentally
  points to elsewhere in the system.
- Con: everywhere that currently joins "record -> entity" by label has to be
  taught to join through the alias table instead; if some join site is
  missed, that site silently regresses to the old bug. You still need a
  reliable way to *populate* the alias table (see Migration below) and a
  reliable way to know an old subject+number entry doesn't collide with
  something reused later (see #3 in the rubric below).

**2. Fuzzy / heuristic matching.** Instead of an explicit alias table, infer
that "old identity X" and "new identity Y" are the same entity by matching
on other signals when subject+number changes — department, unit count,
title/description similarity, instructor overlap, etc.
- Pro: no dependency on the source system giving you a stable id or an
  explicit rename signal; can retroactively "discover" renames from data you
  already have.
- Con: probabilistic — false positives (silently merging two unrelated
  entities because they look similar) are corruption of historical data that
  can be very hard to notice after the fact, since the result looks
  plausible, not obviously broken. False negatives (missing a real rename)
  regress to today's bug. This is the design most likely to introduce a
  worse failure mode than the one being fixed. It's a reasonable *fallback*
  for cases where no authoritative signal exists, but a weak *primary*
  design when a stable id is available or obtainable from the source
  system.

**3. Stable internal id from the start.** Never key any downstream feature
by the mutable label at all. Every feature that needs "this entity's data"
— grades, requirements, reviews, whatever — always joins on an internal
immutable id; the current subject+number is just display metadata attached
to that id.
- Pro: architecturally the cleanest. The rename-tracking problem stops being
  a per-feature concern and becomes a property of the id itself; no feature
  can regress into "oops, joined on the mutable label again" because the
  mutable label was never a valid join key to begin with.
- Con: this is a bigger commitment than a bugfix — it's touching the join
  key for every downstream feature, not just the one that's currently
  broken. If other features already join on subject+number (this is exactly
  what had happened elsewhere in Berkeleytime — `class` and `course`
  resolvers, association logic, frontend URL encoding all had subject+number
  baked in as if it were stable), all of them need to be found and migrated,
  which is a much larger and riskier undertaking than fixing one query. Only
  worth it if you're fairly confident more of these bugs exist or will keep
  appearing — otherwise you're proposing a rearchitecture in response to a
  single reported bug.

**4. Manual curation / mapping table maintained by admins.** Someone with
domain knowledge maintains an explicit "old identity -> new identity"
mapping by hand, keyed on whatever the team already knows about known
renames.
- Pro: lowest engineering cost by a wide margin — no schema changes, no
  fuzzy matching, no rearchitecture. Fast to ship for a small, known set of
  renames.
- Con: doesn't scale, and it's entirely dependent on a human noticing a
  rename happened and being available to update the mapping. Every future
  rename that isn't manually entered reproduces the original bug. Fine as a
  stopgap or for a handful of known cases; not fine as the only mechanism if
  renames are expected to keep happening on an ongoing basis (they are —
  it's routine SIS behavior).

### The central tension: push on #3 vs. #1

This is the discussion that separates strong candidates. A strong candidate
should, unprompted or with one nudge, recognize that #3 is the more
"correct" design in the abstract, but that "more architecturally correct"
and "the right call right now" are different questions. Push on:

- "You've told me #3 is cleaner. Would you actually propose it if this were
  a single bug report about one course showing incomplete grades?" — Good
  candidates say no, or say "only if I also had evidence this same bug
  exists in three other places" — i.e., they scope the fix to the evidence,
  not to architectural purity.
- "What would make you change your mind and go with #3 anyway?" — Good
  answers: this is the Nth time this exact class of bug has shown up across
  different features; the team already has budget/roadmap space for a data
  model migration; the alias-table approach (#1) is visibly leaking into
  every join site anyway, so you're paying most of #3's cost without its
  benefit.
- A candidate who immediately jumps to "rearchitect everything to use
  stable ids" without being asked to weigh cost against a single bug report
  is over-engineering for the stated problem — flag this if they don't walk
  it back when pushed.

### Required follow-up: migration / backfill

Always ask, if the candidate doesn't bring it up unprompted: **"Renames
already happened before your fix ships. How do you backfill history for
those?"**

Strong answers engage with where the mapping actually comes from:
- If the source-of-record system (e.g., the SIS) exposes its own stable
  course identifier, backfilling is mostly a data pull: for each entity,
  pull every historical label it has held from the source system directly
  — no guessing required.
- If no such stable id is available/exposed, the candidate should recognize
  this degrades toward design #2 or #4 for the backfill step specifically
  (heuristic matching, or manual review of a candidate list of "these old
  labels look like they might be renames of these current labels") — and
  should say explicitly that this is lower-confidence than the id-based
  case, and describe how they'd bound the risk (e.g., require a human to
  confirm inferred renames above some ambiguity threshold before they go
  live).
- Bonus: candidate distinguishes "renames that happened before we ever
  started keeping this history" (potentially unrecoverable if no
  intermediate signal survived) from "renames that happened after we had
  some other historical process running" (potentially recoverable by
  correlating dates in the historical records with the timeline of the
  rename).

### Red flags

- Candidate assumes subject+number (or the local system's version of "the
  display label") is a stable primary key without being prompted to
  reconsider — i.e., initial design has no separate stable id at all, and
  they don't catch it themselves when describing how a rename would be
  handled.
- No mention of backfill/migration at all, even after the direct
  follow-up question above.
- Treats fuzzy matching (#2) as if it were as safe as an explicit id/alias
  approach — doesn't independently raise the false-positive risk (silently
  merging two unrelated entities) as a distinct and more dangerous failure
  mode than a false negative.
- Proposes #3 (full rearchitecture) as the *only* acceptable answer to a
  single bug report, with no cost/scope discussion.
- Doesn't consider the "number gets reused by an unrelated entity later"
  collision case at all, even when asked directly (prompt 3 in the
  candidate doc).

## Round 2: Implementation code review guide

### What the tests check

`getGradeHistoryForCourse` ships as a stub (`throw new Error("not
implemented")`), so all 6 tests in `impl/test/gradeHistory.test.ts` fail
before a candidate writes anything. Here's what each one verifies about a
*correct* implementation, and why it's in the suite:

- **Never-renamed control case** (`course-61a`) — the baseline: a course
  with only one identity should just return all of its records. Any
  implementation that fails this is broken at the most basic level (e.g.
  querying the wrong field, off-by-one in a filter).
- **Unknown course id** — returns `[]` rather than throwing or returning
  everything. Checks that the "no matching course" path is handled
  explicitly, not just assumed away.
- **Single rename** (`course-astron`, ASTRON 88 -> ASTRON 128) — the
  minimum case that actually exercises rename-following: two records are
  filed under the old identity and two under the new one, and all four must
  come back. An implementation that only looks up the course's current
  subject+number fails this outright.
- **Single rename, exact count + number check** — same course, but asserts
  exactly 4 records come back and that every one of them is numbered "88" or
  "128". This is the one that catches *overcorrection*: an implementation
  that relaxes the match to subject-only (dropping the number check
  entirely) would pull in the unrelated noise row (`ASTRON 10`) too — length
  would be 5, not 4, and the "every number is 88 or 128" check would fail.
- **Double rename, chained** (`course-ethstd`, LEGALST 21 -> AMERSTD 21AC ->
  ETHSTD 21AC) — records under all three identities must come back. This is
  the test that catches an implementation that special-cases "current +
  one previous identity" instead of generalizing to arbitrary rename counts:
  it would pass the single-rename test above but fail this one, since
  `course-ethstd` has two *prior* identities, not one.
- **Enrollment aggregation across renames** — sums `enrolled` across all of
  `course-ethstd`'s records and checks the total (350). This is a
  correctness check on the same underlying set as the double-rename test,
  from a different angle (a candidate could get the right *count* of
  records but the wrong *set*, e.g. by mismatching term ranges — this
  catches that).

### One correct approach

There's more than one reasonable implementation here — candidates aren't
expected to converge on this exact one — but here's a reference solution to
calibrate against: for a given `courseId`, look up every row in
`courseIdentityHistory` for that `courseId` (that's the full set of
subject+number identities the course has ever held, current one included),
then filter `gradeDistributions` for rows matching *any* of those
identities.

```ts
export function getGradeHistoryForCourse(courseId: string): GradeRecord[] {
  const identities = courseIdentityHistory.filter(
    (i) => i.courseId === courseId
  );
  if (identities.length === 0) return [];

  return gradeDistributions.filter((g) =>
    identities.some((i) => i.subject === g.subject && i.number === g.number)
  );
}
```

This is sufficient to pass the suite. Things to look for beyond "does it
pass":

- **Correctly generalizes past one rename.** The fixtures include a
  double-renamed course specifically to catch an implementation that
  special-cases "look at current identity + one previous identity" instead
  of iterating the full history. An implementation hardcoded to exactly one
  prior identity will pass the single-rename test but fail the
  double-rename one — watch for this if a candidate writes something like
  `course.subject === g.subject || course.previousSubject === g.subject`
  instead of consulting `courseIdentityHistory` (or an equivalent structure
  they built) generally.
- **Doesn't regress to subject-only matching.** An implementation that
  filters `gradeDistributions` by subject alone (dropping the number check
  entirely) would incorrectly pull in the unrelated-course noise rows in the
  fixtures and fail that test. Ask a candidate who does this to explain why
  matching subject alone is unsafe (a subject can have many unrelated course
  numbers under it).
- **Efficiency, for a candidate who wants to talk about it.** The reference
  solution is O(courses × gradeDistributions) in the worst case with the
  naive nested `.some()`. At fixture scale this is irrelevant; at real scale
  you'd want to index `gradeDistributions` by `subject|number` once up
  front (or better, resolve the identity set once and use a `Set` for O(1)
  membership checks) rather than doing a linear scan with `.some()` inside
  a `.filter()`. This is not required to pass the tests — don't dock a
  candidate for not doing it — but it's a good discussion point and a
  strong signal if a candidate raises it unprompted (mirrors the actual
  Berkeleytime fix, where the real solution was to change what field a
  MongoDB query filtered on, i.e., push the join down into an index rather
  than doing it in application code at all).
- **Doesn't mutate or restructure the fixtures/tests.** The task explicitly
  asks candidates not to change the test file or fixtures. A candidate who
  "fixes" a failing test by loosening its assertion, or by adding data to
  the fixtures to make their implementation's behavior match, has not
  actually solved the problem — flag this clearly, it's a meaningfully
  different (and concerning) signal from an honest implementation.

### AI-tool-usage questions to ask at debrief

- "Walk me through your prompt log — what was the first thing you asked
  for?" Look for whether they gave the AI tool the actual contract (JSDoc +
  fixtures + test expectations, rename-following across arbitrary counts)
  or whether they pasted just the function signature and got back something
  generic that happened to look plausible without understanding why it did
  or didn't work.
- "Did the AI's first draft handle multiple renames correctly on its own,
  or only the single-rename case?" This is the most common failure mode:
  first-draft AI output frequently special-cases "current identity + one
  previous identity" and passes the single-rename test while failing the
  double-rename one. A candidate who ran the tests, noticed the
  double-rename case fail, and iterated is behaving well. A candidate who
  didn't notice a partial implementation still left a test red is a red
  flag regardless of whether AI or their own hand wrote the code.
- "Where did you disagree with or change what the AI produced?" Candidates
  with no answer here at all — full acceptance of the first suggestion,
  no edits — are worth probing further on whether they actually understood
  the implementation or are relying on green tests as their only signal of
  correctness.

### Red flags (Round 2)

- All tests pass but the candidate can't explain, unprompted, *why* their
  implementation needs to consult more than a course's current identity
  (i.e., can't articulate the rename-following requirement in their own
  words).
- Implementation is special-cased to the fixture data rather than general
  (e.g., hardcodes `"ASTRON"` or checks `courseId === "course-ethstd"`
  somewhere).
- Doesn't run the test suite at all before declaring done, or doesn't
  notice/investigate when some tests still fail.
- Edits the test file or fixtures to make failing tests pass instead of
  fixing the implementation.

---

## Rubric (score each 1-5)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| System design judgment | Assumes label is stable; no alternative designs offered | Names 2+ designs but doesn't compare tradeoffs concretely | Compares designs on their actual failure modes (collision risk, migration cost, blast radius) and picks one with reasoning |
| Code quality / correctness | Fix is fixture-specific or leaves tests failing | Fix is general and passes all tests but is inefficient or unclear | General, correct, reasonably efficient, and clearly explains why the old code broke |
| Tradeoff articulation | Treats one design as obviously "the" answer | Lists pros/cons but doesn't engage when pushed | Updates or defends position under direct pushback with real reasoning (not just "it depends") |
| AI-tool usage judgment | Accepts first AI output uncritically, can't say what they changed | Iterates on AI output but only because tests told them to | Gives AI tools good context, catches subtle issues (e.g., partial rename handling) independently, can explain every line they kept |
| Communication | Hard to follow; jumps between ideas without landing conclusions | Clear but needs prompting to get to tradeoffs | Concise, leads with a position, and clearly flags what's uncertain vs. settled |

## Time budget

- Round 1: 45-60 minutes. Budget ~10 min setup/framing, ~30-40 min design +
  discussion, ~5-10 min migration follow-up if not already covered.
- Round 2: 3-4 hours, typically done independently/asynchronously with a
  15-20 minute debrief/code-review conversation afterward covering the
  "what a correct fix looks like" and "AI usage" sections above.
